title: Prompt Engineering
description: The single highest-leverage skill in the course: getting reliable output from a model.

lessons.title: What a prompt is
lessons.description: Everything you send, not just the question you type.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A prompt is everything you send to the model. That is the whole definition, and it is broader than most people assume.

It is not only your question. It includes any standing instruction the tool adds, the conversation so far, any document you pasted, and any examples you gave. All of it arrives as one block of text, and the model predicts what follows.

### Why this is worth saying carefully

If you think a prompt is "the question you type", you will try to improve results by rewording the question. That is the smallest lever available.

If you understand the prompt is everything sent, you start using the larger levers: supplying the source material, giving examples, setting constraints, defining the format. Those change results far more than rewording ever will.

### The two halves

Most tools split what you send into two parts.

The **system prompt** sets standing behaviour: who the assistant is, what it should always do, what it must never do. You may see it called custom instructions, a persona, or project instructions. It applies to the whole conversation.

The **user prompt** is your actual request, this time.

The distinction is not just organisational. Instructions in the system prompt tend to be followed more consistently and are less likely to be pushed aside by a long conversation.

### Prompt engineering is not magic words

There is a great deal of folklore about phrases that unlock hidden ability. Most of it is nonsense, and the rest stops working with the next model release.

What actually works is unglamorous:

- Say clearly what you want
- Supply the material rather than relying on recall
- Show an example of a good answer
- State the constraints, including the format
- Check the output and adjust

That is the whole discipline. The rest of this module is those five things in detail.

### One thing genuinely worth internalising

**The model cannot ask you what you meant.** It produces a best guess in one shot. Everything ambiguous in your prompt gets resolved by the model, in a direction you did not choose.

So the skill is largely about removing ambiguity before you send. Not writing more -- writing less that can be read two ways.

## Demonstrate

Watch a prompt improve in three steps. Run each one; the difference is the lesson.

**Attempt one.**

> Write about renewable energy.

You get a few hundred words of encyclopedia. Correct, generic, useless for anything in particular.

**Attempt two.** Add audience and purpose.

> Write a short piece about renewable energy for a college newsletter, aimed at students who are not studying science.

Better. Now it is pitched at someone.

**Attempt three.** Add constraints, format and an angle.

> Write a 200-word piece for a college newsletter about why renewable energy matters for students specifically. Audience: non-science undergraduates. Include one concrete example involving campus electricity costs. Plain language, no jargon. End with one thing a student could actually do. No headings, no bullet points.

Now you get something usable in one attempt.

Notice what changed. Not the politeness, not any magic phrase. Audience, purpose, length, content requirement, tone, ending, format. Seven pieces of information the model previously had to guess.

## Practice

Take the vaguest AI request you have made recently. If you cannot remember one, use "help me write an email".

Rewrite it, adding each of these in turn, running the prompt after each addition and keeping the output:

1. Who the audience is
2. What it is for
3. How long it should be
4. One thing it must include
5. The format

Five versions. Put the first and last side by side.

Almost everyone finds the improvement much larger than expected, and gets there without a single clever phrase.

## What to remember

- A prompt is everything sent to the model, not just your question
- System prompts set standing behaviour; user prompts are this request
- Prompt engineering is clarity and context, not magic words
- The model cannot ask what you meant, so it guesses
- The skill is removing ambiguity, not adding length

lessons.title: The anatomy of a good prompt
lessons.description: Six parts, and the one line that does most for reliability.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A reliable prompt has parts. Not every prompt needs all of them, but knowing the list means you can check what is missing when output disappoints.

### The six parts

**1. Role.** Who the model should be. *"You are an experienced technical recruiter."* Sets vocabulary and perspective. Optional, and covered properly in lesson 4.

**2. Task.** What to do, as a clear instruction. This is the one people include. *"Review this CV against the job description below."*

**3. Context.** The material and background. The job description, the document, the audience, the situation. **This is usually the biggest win and the most commonly missing part.**

**4. Constraints.** The boundaries. Length, tone, what to include, what to avoid, what to do when unsure. *"Under 300 words. No jargon. If the CV does not mention something, say so rather than inferring it."*

**5. Format.** The shape of the output. Prose, bullets, a table, JSON, a specific set of headings. Say it explicitly; the default is whatever the model feels like.

**6. Examples.** One or more worked cases. The most powerful and least used part, covered in lesson 3.

### The order that works

Put **context before the instruction** when the context is long.

There is a practical reason. In a long prompt, the instruction is easier for the model to act on when it comes after the material it applies to -- the model has just read the material and then learns what to do with it. Leading with a long document and burying the instruction three thousand words back works noticeably less well.

A structure that holds up:

```
[Role, if any]

[Context: documents, background, audience]

[Task: what to do]

[Constraints: boundaries]

[Format: shape of output]

[Examples, if any]
```

### Say what to do, not only what not to do

"Do not be verbose" is weaker than "under 150 words". "Do not use jargon" is weaker than "use language a fifteen-year-old would follow".

A negative instruction tells the model which region to avoid and leaves everything else open. A positive one names the target. Where you can convert a prohibition into a specification, do.

Some prohibitions have no positive form -- "do not invent citations" is worth keeping. Use both where both help.

### Handle the uncertain case explicitly

The single most valuable constraint, and almost nobody includes it:

> If the information needed is not in the material provided, say so explicitly rather than filling the gap.

Without this, a gap in your context gets filled with a plausible invention. With it, you get told. This one line does more for reliability than any amount of rewording.

## Demonstrate

The same job, before and after.

**Before.**

> Summarise this report.

**After.**

> Below is a quarterly report from our logistics team.
>
> [report text]
>
> Summarise it for the senior leadership team, who have not read it and have two minutes.
>
> Requirements:
> - Under 200 words
> - Lead with the single most important finding
> - Include any number that changed by more than 10 per cent
> - Flag anything that needs a decision from leadership
> - If the report does not state something clearly, say so rather than inferring it
>
> Format: one short opening paragraph, then a bulleted list of at most five points.

Every part is present: context first, then task, constraints, the uncertainty instruction, format.

The second takes ninety seconds longer to write and saves three rounds of correction. That trade is the whole argument for this lesson.

## Practice

Take a prompt you have written that gave disappointing output.

Go through the six parts and mark each present or missing. Most disappointing prompts are missing context, constraints and format -- often all three.

Rewrite it with every applicable part, in the order above, including the uncertainty instruction. Run both. Keep them side by side.

Then write one sentence on which addition made the biggest difference. For most people it is context.

## What to remember

- Six parts: role, task, context, constraints, format, examples
- Missing context is the most common cause of disappointing output
- Put long context before the instruction
- Convert prohibitions into specifications where you can
- Always tell the model what to do when the information is not there

lessons.title: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting
lessons.description: Showing beats describing, and when it is worth the context.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**Zero-shot** means asking without examples. You describe the task and the model does it.

**Few-shot** means including worked examples in the prompt. You show two, three or five cases of input and the output you want, then give the real input.

That is the whole distinction, and few-shot is dramatically underused.

### Why examples work so well

A language model predicts continuations. When your prompt contains three examples of a pattern, the most likely continuation is a fourth item following that pattern.

You are not teaching the model anything -- remember, it does not learn from your prompt. You are making the pattern you want the overwhelmingly obvious thing to produce next.

This is why examples often succeed where instructions fail. It is much easier to demonstrate a tone than to describe it.

### When to use which

**Zero-shot** for common, well-defined tasks. Summarise this, translate this, explain this, fix this grammar. The model has seen these patterns many times and does not need your help.

**Few-shot** when:

- The output format is specific and unusual
- The tone is particular and hard to describe
- The task involves your own categories or conventions
- The judgement is subtle and easier to show than state
- Zero-shot nearly worked but drifted

That last one is the most common real trigger. When you find yourself writing a fourth paragraph of description trying to pin down what you want, stop and show two examples instead.

### Writing examples that work

**Two to five.** One is often read as a one-off. Beyond five, returns drop and you are spending context.

**Make them realistic.** Toy examples produce toy-quality output. Use real cases, anonymised if needed.

**Cover the variety, including the awkward cases.** If some inputs are messy, include a messy one. If some have no good answer, include one and show what you want then. Examples that are all easy teach the model your task is easy.

**Keep the formatting identical across examples.** Any inconsistency is a pattern too, and the model may follow it.

**Watch for accidental patterns.** If all three of your examples happen to produce three bullet points, you have implicitly required three bullet points. If all your example inputs are short, you may get poor results on long ones.

### A format that works

```
Input: [example input 1]
Output: [desired output 1]

Input: [example input 2]
Output: [desired output 2]

Input: [the real one]
Output:
```

Simple, unambiguous, and the trailing label makes the continuation obvious.

## Demonstrate

A task where zero-shot reliably underperforms: classifying support messages into a company's own categories.

**Zero-shot.**

> Classify this support message as Billing, Technical, Account or Other: "I was charged twice for last month."

This one works, because the case is clear. Now try: *"It keeps logging me out every time I try to update my card."* Billing or Technical? The model picks one. You do not know which convention it used, and it may pick differently tomorrow.

**Few-shot**, with the awkward cases shown:

```
Classify each message as Billing, Technical, Account or Other.
When a message involves both payment and a fault, classify by the
fault, because our billing team cannot fix faults.

Message: I was charged twice for last month.
Category: Billing

Message: It keeps logging me out when I try to update my card.
Category: Technical

Message: Can you change the email on my account?
Category: Account

Message: Your competitor is cheaper.
Category: Other

Message: The payment page shows an error after I click submit.
Category:
```

The second example is doing the real work. It shows the exact ambiguous case and resolves it, and it states the rule behind the resolution. You now get your convention rather than the model's.

## Practice

Take a task where you have specific conventions -- how your team categorises things, formats notes, writes summaries, replies to certain requests.

Write it zero-shot and run it on five real inputs. Record how many matched your convention.

Now write a few-shot version with three examples, including at least one genuinely awkward case. Run the same five inputs. Record again.

Write one sentence on what the examples fixed that the instructions could not.

## What to remember

- Zero-shot is no examples; few-shot includes worked cases
- Examples make your pattern the obvious continuation
- Use few-shot for specific formats, particular tone, your own conventions, and subtle judgement
- Two to five realistic examples, including the awkward cases
- Watch for accidental patterns your examples create

lessons.title: Role prompting
lessons.description: A tone control, not a capability upgrade.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Role prompting means telling the model who to be. *"You are a patient maths tutor."* *"You are a careful copy editor."* *"Respond as an experienced paediatric nurse would."*

It works, within limits, and the limits are what this lesson is about.

### What it actually does

A role shifts which region of language the model draws on. Text written by copy editors looks different from text written by marketers: different vocabulary, different concerns, different level of detail, different things left unsaid.

Naming a role makes that kind of text the likely continuation.

### What it does not do

**It does not add knowledge.** "You are a cardiologist" does not give the model medical knowledge it lacked. It changes the style in which it produces what it already had. A confidently-worded wrong answer in medical register is more dangerous than the same wrong answer in ordinary language, not less.

**It does not add reliability.** "You are a fact-checker who never makes mistakes" does not reduce hallucination. It may make the output sound more authoritative, which is worse.

**It does not confer authority.** Nothing about the role makes the answer more likely to be correct.

Treat role prompting as a **tone and perspective control**. That is a real and useful thing. It is not a capability upgrade, and people routinely mistake it for one.

### Roles that earn their place

**Setting expertise level for the explanation.** *"Explain this as you would to a first-year undergraduate."* Genuinely useful, because it is about the audience.

**Setting a professional register.** *"You are a technical writer. Prefer short sentences and the active voice."*

**Setting a perspective deliberately.** *"Review this plan as a sceptical finance director would."* Useful because it surfaces objections you might not think of.

**Setting a relationship.** *"You are a tutor. Do not give the answer. Ask a question that helps me find it."* This one changes behaviour meaningfully, because it constrains what the model may do.

Notice the pattern: the useful roles specify **audience, register, perspective or behaviour**. The useless ones claim expertise and hope.

### The stronger version

Instead of claiming a role, describe the behaviour you want:

Weak: *"You are an expert editor."*

Strong: *"Edit for clarity. Prefer short sentences. Cut every word that does not change the meaning. Do not alter quotations. Where a sentence is ambiguous, flag it rather than guessing what I meant."*

The second is longer and far more reliable, because every clause is actionable. The first is a wish.

Use a role as shorthand when it genuinely carries the meaning, and spell out behaviour when precision matters.

## Demonstrate

The same question, three ways. Run all three and compare.

**No role.**

> Explain why interest rates affect house prices.

**Role, claiming expertise.**

> You are a senior economist. Explain why interest rates affect house prices.

**Role, specifying audience and behaviour.**

> Explain why interest rates affect house prices to someone buying their first home, who has never studied economics. Use one worked example with round numbers. Avoid technical terms; where one is unavoidable, define it in the same sentence. Under 250 words.

The second is usually more technical and less useful than the first -- the expertise claim made the writing denser without making it more correct.

The third is the one you would actually send to someone. And it never claimed any expertise at all.

## Practice

Take a concept from your own field that you often have to explain.

Write three prompts: no role, an expertise role, and one specifying audience plus behaviour with no expertise claim.

Run all three. Then show the outputs to someone who does not know the field and ask which they understood best.

Most people find the third wins, and find that result mildly annoying, having spent time on elaborate expertise personas.

## What to remember

- A role shifts tone and perspective, not knowledge or reliability
- Claiming expertise can make wrong answers sound more authoritative
- The useful roles specify audience, register, perspective or behaviour
- Describing behaviour beats claiming a role when precision matters
- "Explain it to X" is usually more effective than "you are an expert Y"

lessons.title: Chain of thought
lessons.description: Give the model room to work, then read the working.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Chain of thought means getting the model to work through a problem in steps before producing an answer, rather than answering immediately.

The classic instruction is *"think step by step"*, and for certain problems it makes a real difference.

### Why it works

A model produces text one token at a time, each conditioned on everything before it. When it jumps straight to an answer, that answer is produced without any intermediate work existing to condition on.

When it writes out the steps first, each step becomes part of the context for the next. The reasoning is in the text, and the final answer is produced in the presence of it.

Put plainly: **the model's working is not hidden, it is the output**. Give it room to produce working and the answer tends to improve.

### Where it helps

- Arithmetic and quantitative word problems
- Multi-step logic
- Anything with several constraints that interact
- Debugging, where the fault has to be located before it can be fixed
- Decisions that need several factors weighed

### Where it does not help

- Simple lookups and classification
- Creative writing, where it often makes output stilted
- Anything where you want a short answer and the working is noise
- Tasks that are genuinely one step

Applying it everywhere wastes tokens and time, and makes the output worse for short tasks.

### A caution that matters

**The stated reasoning is not necessarily the real reasoning.**

The model generates plausible-looking steps. Those steps influence the answer, which is why the technique works. But a chain of thought can be internally consistent, convincing, and wrong -- and it can arrive at a right answer through steps that do not hold up.

So read the steps. Do not treat their presence as proof. A confident, well-structured, wrong derivation is a real and common output.

### Modern models and the instruction

Many current models already do a form of this internally, and some expose it as a setting rather than something you prompt for. The explicit instruction matters less than it once did.

What still helps, and will keep helping, is **asking for the working to be shown** when you want to check it, and **structuring the steps yourself** when you know what they should be.

### The stronger version: name the steps

Rather than "think step by step", give the steps:

> Work through this in order:
> 1. List every constraint stated in the brief
> 2. For each option, note which constraints it meets and which it fails
> 3. Identify any constraint no option meets
> 4. Recommend one option and state what it gives up
>
> Show your work for each step before the recommendation.

This is more reliable than the generic instruction, because you have supplied the structure rather than hoping a useful one appears.

## Demonstrate

A problem where the difference is visible.

> A shop sells notebooks at 40 rupees each. If you buy 5 or more you get 15 per cent off the whole order. Priya buys 4 notebooks, then realises she needs 3 more and buys them in a separate transaction. How much more would she have saved by buying all 7 together?

Ask it directly and you may get a confidently wrong number -- there are several plausible wrong answers, such as forgetting that neither transaction alone qualified for the discount.

Now ask with structure:

> Work through this in order, showing each step:
> 1. Cost of the first transaction, and whether it qualified for the discount
> 2. Cost of the second transaction, and whether it qualified
> 3. Total actually paid
> 4. Cost of buying all 7 together, including any discount
> 5. The difference
>
> Then state the final answer.

The accuracy improves noticeably. And crucially, when it is wrong you can now see **where** it went wrong, which you could not before.

That second benefit is underrated. Visible working is checkable working.

## Practice

Find a problem in your own field with several steps -- a calculation, a decision with competing constraints, a diagnosis.

Ask it three ways:

1. Direct, answer only
2. With "think step by step"
3. With the steps named by you

Check all three against the right answer, which you should work out yourself first.

Then read the working in versions 2 and 3. Look specifically for a step that is stated confidently and is wrong. Most people find one within a few attempts, and it is the most instructive thing in the exercise.

## What to remember

- Writing out the steps gives the model something to condition on, improving hard answers
- It helps on multi-step reasoning and hurts on simple or creative tasks
- The stated reasoning is not proof of the real reasoning; read it
- Naming the steps yourself beats the generic instruction
- Visible working is checkable working, which is worth as much as the accuracy gain

lessons.title: Asking for structured output
lessons.description: JSON a program can read, and the rule that stops invented values.
lessons.content:
## Learn

If a person reads the output, prose is fine. If a **program** reads the output, prose is a problem.

Structured output means asking the model to reply in a machine-readable format -- usually JSON -- so the next step can use it without a human in between.

### Why this matters more than it sounds

The moment you want to do anything automatic with model output -- put it in a spreadsheet, store it in a database, route it somewhere, count it -- you need structure. Every real application in modules 12 to 14 depends on this.

### How to ask for it

Three things make it reliable.

**1. Show the exact shape.** Do not describe the JSON; write it out.

**2. Say what to do about missing values.** Otherwise the model invents a value or silently drops the key.

**3. Say "only the JSON, no other text".** Without this you frequently get a friendly sentence before and after, which breaks parsing.

```
Extract the details from the email below.

Return ONLY a JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:

{
  "sender_name": string or null,
  "company": string or null,
  "request_type": one of "quote", "support", "complaint", "other",
  "urgency": one of "low", "medium", "high",
  "deadline": "YYYY-MM-DD" or null
}

If a field is not stated in the email, use null. Do not infer it.

Email:
[email text]
```

### The rule that prevents most damage

**"If it is not stated, use null. Do not infer."**

Without that line, a model handed an email with no deadline will often produce a plausible one. You will not notice, because the JSON parses perfectly and the value looks reasonable.

This is hallucination in a form that is much harder to catch, because the structure gives it an air of having been extracted rather than generated.

### Always validate

Even with a perfect prompt, do not trust the shape. Validate before use.

Several providers offer a strict structured-output mode that guarantees the response matches a schema. Where your tool has it, use it -- it removes a whole class of problem. Where it does not, validate yourself, which is the exercise below.

## Demonstrate

```python
import json
import os

# The key is read from the environment. Never write a key into a file.
API_KEY = os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"]

PROMPT = """Extract the details from the email below.

Return ONLY a JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:

{{
  "sender_name": string or null,
  "company": string or null,
  "request_type": one of "quote", "support", "complaint", "other",
  "urgency": one of "low", "medium", "high"
}}

If a field is not stated in the email, use null. Do not infer it.

Email:
{email}
"""


def parse_response(raw: str) -> dict:
    """Turn a model response into a dict, tolerating stray prose."""
    # Models sometimes wrap JSON in a markdown fence despite instructions.
    text = raw.strip()
    if text.startswith("```"):
        text = text.split("```")[1]
        if text.startswith("json"):
            text = text[4:]
    return json.loads(text.strip())
```

Note the defensive parsing. The prompt says "only JSON". Most of the time that is honoured. The code assumes it sometimes will not be, which is the correct posture for anything a model produces.

## Practice

### Exercise: validate an extraction

Write a function that checks a parsed response against the expected shape, returning a list of problems. It must catch: missing keys, unexpected keys, wrong types, and values outside an allowed set.

```python
def validate_extraction(data: dict) -> list[str]:
    """Check a parsed extraction against the expected shape.

    Returns a list of human-readable problems. An empty list means the
    data is usable.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for a good record:

```
[]
```

Expected output for `{"sender_name": "Ana", "company": None, "request_type": "invoice", "urgency": "high", "extra": 1}`:

```
["unexpected key: extra", "request_type must be one of ['quote', 'support', 'complaint', 'other'], got 'invoice'"]
```

:::hint Getting started
Define the expected keys and the allowed values as module-level constants first. Then check in three passes: keys present, no unexpected keys, then per-field type and allowed values. Collect problems in a list rather than returning on the first one -- a caller wants all of them at once.
:::

:::solution
```python
ALLOWED = {
    "request_type": ["quote", "support", "complaint", "other"],
    "urgency": ["low", "medium", "high"],
}
EXPECTED_KEYS = {"sender_name", "company", "request_type", "urgency"}
NULLABLE = {"sender_name", "company"}


def validate_extraction(data: dict) -> list[str]:
    """Check a parsed extraction against the expected shape."""
    problems = []

    for key in sorted(EXPECTED_KEYS - set(data)):
        problems.append(f"missing key: {key}")
    for key in sorted(set(data) - EXPECTED_KEYS):
        problems.append(f"unexpected key: {key}")

    for key in sorted(EXPECTED_KEYS & set(data)):
        value = data[key]
        if value is None:
            if key not in NULLABLE:
                problems.append(f"{key} must not be null")
            continue
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            problems.append(f"{key} must be a string, got {type(value).__name__}")
        elif key in ALLOWED and value not in ALLOWED[key]:
            problems.append(f"{key} must be one of {ALLOWED[key]}, got {value!r}")

    return problems


if __name__ == "__main__":
    good = {"sender_name": "Ana", "company": None, "request_type": "quote", "urgency": "high"}
    bad = {"sender_name": "Ana", "company": None, "request_type": "invoice", "urgency": "high", "extra": 1}
    print(validate_extraction(good))
    print(validate_extraction(bad))
```

Output:

```
[]
['unexpected key: extra', "request_type must be one of ['quote', 'support', 'complaint', 'other'], got 'invoice'"]
```

Two deliberate choices. The keys are sorted so the output is stable, which matters the moment you write a test against it. And `continue` after the null check avoids a confusing second complaint about a null value's type.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This function is meant to extract the first JSON object from a response that may have prose around it. It has **two** bugs.

```python
import json


def extract_json(raw: str) -> dict:
    start = raw.find("{")
    end = raw.find("}")
    if start == -1:
        raise ValueError("no JSON object found")
    return json.loads(raw[start:end])
```

:::hint What to look at
Try it on a response containing a nested object, such as `{"a": {"b": 1}}`. Then check the slice boundaries carefully against what `find` returns.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: it finds the first closing brace, not the last.** On `{"a": {"b": 1}}` it stops at the inner `}` and produces invalid JSON. Use `rfind("}")` to get the last one.

**Bug two: the slice excludes the closing brace.** `raw[start:end]` stops one character short, so even on flat objects the result is missing its final `}`. It needs `end + 1`.

```python
import json


def extract_json(raw: str) -> dict:
    """Extract the outermost JSON object from a response."""
    start = raw.find("{")
    end = raw.rfind("}")
    if start == -1 or end == -1 or end < start:
        raise ValueError("no JSON object found")
    return json.loads(raw[start : end + 1])
```

The added `end < start` guard matters: a response containing `}` before `{` would otherwise produce a negative-length slice and a confusing parse error rather than a clear one.

Bug one is the instructive one. The function works on every flat test object you are likely to write by hand, and fails the first time a real response nests anything. Test data that is simpler than production data hides exactly this kind of fault.
:::

## What to remember

- Prose is fine for people and a problem for programs
- Show the exact shape rather than describing it, and say "only the JSON"
- Always include "if it is not stated, use null, do not infer"
- Structure makes invented values look extracted, which is harder to catch
- Validate the shape before use, even when the prompt was perfect

lessons.title: Prompt templates
lessons.description: Write the good prompt once, then fill in the holes.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A prompt template is a prompt with holes in it. You write the good version once, mark the parts that change, and fill them in each time.

This is the step between using AI as a toy and using it as a tool.

### Why bother

**Consistency.** The same prompt gives comparable output every time. Ad-hoc prompts give varying quality and you cannot tell whether a change in output came from the input or from how you happened to phrase it.

**Improvement compounds.** Fix the template once and every future use benefits. Ad-hoc prompts mean re-learning the same lessons.

**It can be shared.** A good template is a small piece of institutional knowledge. One person works out how to get reliable meeting summaries and everyone gets them.

**It can be tested.** A fixed template with varying inputs can be evaluated, which is the next lesson. A prompt you retype each time cannot.

### What goes in a template

Everything from the anatomy lesson, with the variable parts marked:

```
You are summarising a meeting for people who did not attend.

Meeting: {meeting_name}
Date: {date}
Attendees: {attendees}

Transcript:
{transcript}

Produce:
1. A one-sentence summary
2. Decisions made, as a bulleted list
3. Action items, each with an owner and a date if one was stated

Rules:
- Under {word_limit} words total
- Use only what is in the transcript
- If an action has no clear owner, write "owner not stated" rather than guessing
- If there were no decisions, say so rather than inventing one
```

The fixed part carries all the quality. The holes carry only the facts that change.

### Rules that keep templates working

**Put the instructions in the fixed part.** If a caller has to remember to add "be concise", it is not in the template.

**Name the holes clearly.** `{transcript}` not `{text}`. Readable names prevent the wrong thing being passed.

**Handle the empty case.** What if the transcript is empty, or the attendee list is unknown? Decide, and put it in the template.

**Version it.** When you change a template, note what changed and why. Otherwise you will improve it, make it worse, and have no way back.

### The mistake everyone makes once

Building the template around one example input.

You write it while looking at a single transcript, it works beautifully on that transcript, and it falls apart on the next one because that one had no decisions, or three people with the same first name, or was in two languages.

Build against three or four genuinely different inputs from the start, including an awkward one.

## Demonstrate

Here is a template as working code, with the two mistakes that break templates in practice already handled.

```python
from string import Template

# Template rather than str.format: the prompt contains JSON examples with
# braces, and .format would try to interpret them as fields.
MEETING_SUMMARY = Template("""You are summarising a meeting for people who did not attend.

Meeting: $meeting_name
Date: $date
Attendees: $attendees

Transcript:
$transcript

Produce:
1. A one-sentence summary
2. Decisions made, as a bulleted list
3. Action items, each with an owner and a date if one was stated

Rules:
- Under $word_limit words total
- Use only what is in the transcript
- If an action has no clear owner, write "owner not stated" rather than guessing
- If there were no decisions, say so rather than inventing one
""")


def build_meeting_prompt(
    meeting_name: str,
    date: str,
    transcript: str,
    attendees: list[str] | None = None,
    word_limit: int = 250,
) -> str:
    """Fill the meeting summary template."""
    if not transcript.strip():
        raise ValueError("transcript is empty; there is nothing to summarise")

    return MEETING_SUMMARY.substitute(
        meeting_name=meeting_name,
        date=date,
        attendees=", ".join(attendees) if attendees else "not recorded",
        transcript=transcript,
        word_limit=word_limit,
    )
```

Two things worth noticing. `string.Template` is used instead of `str.format` because prompts very often contain literal braces -- JSON examples especially -- and `format` would choke on them. And the empty transcript raises immediately rather than sending a prompt that would produce a confident summary of nothing.

## Practice

### Exercise: a template with required and optional fields

Write a small template class that fills a prompt, raises clearly on missing required values, and applies defaults for optional ones.

```python
from string import Template


class PromptTemplate:
    """A prompt template with required and optional fields."""

    def __init__(self, text: str, required: list[str], defaults: dict | None = None):
        # Your code here
        ...

    def render(self, **values) -> str:
        """Fill the template. Raises ValueError naming every missing field."""
        # Your code here
        ...
```

Expected output for a template needing `name` and `topic`, rendered with only `name`:

```
ValueError: missing required field(s): topic
```

:::hint Getting started
Store the text as a `Template`, the required list, and the defaults. In `render`, merge defaults with the supplied values (supplied wins), then compute which required names are absent from the merged dict. Collect all missing names and raise once, rather than raising on the first.
:::

:::solution
```python
from string import Template


class PromptTemplate:
    """A prompt template with required and optional fields."""

    def __init__(self, text: str, required: list[str], defaults: dict | None = None):
        self._template = Template(text)
        self._required = list(required)
        self._defaults = dict(defaults or {})

    def render(self, **values) -> str:
        """Fill the template. Raises ValueError naming every missing field."""
        merged = {**self._defaults, **values}

        missing = [name for name in self._required if not merged.get(name)]
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"missing required field(s): {', '.join(missing)}")

        return self._template.substitute(merged)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = PromptTemplate(
        "Explain $topic to $name in $words words.",
        required=["name", "topic"],
        defaults={"words": 200},
    )
    print(t.render(name="a beginner", topic="tokenization"))
    t.render(name="a beginner")   # raises, naming `topic`
```

Output:

```
Explain tokenization to a beginner in 200 words.
ValueError: missing required field(s): topic
```

`not merged.get(name)` rather than `name not in merged` is deliberate: an empty string passed for a required field is a bug too, and it would otherwise render a prompt with a blank where the topic should be. `dict(defaults or {})` copies the defaults so a caller cannot mutate them through the object later.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This helper is meant to fill a template and warn about unused values. It has **two** bugs.

```python
from string import Template


def render(text: str, values: dict) -> str:
    template = Template(text)
    used = {name for name in values if "$" + name in text}
    unused = used - set(values)
    if unused:
        print(f"warning: unused values: {unused}")
    return template.safe_substitute(values)
```

:::hint What to look at
Two separate things. First, work out what `used - set(values)` can ever contain, given how `used` was built. Second, think about what `safe_substitute` does when a field is missing, and whether that is what you want in a prompt.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: the set subtraction is backwards, and can only ever be empty.** `used` is built from `values`, so `used` is always a subset of `set(values)`, making `used - set(values)` always empty -- the warning never fires. It should be `set(values) - used`.

**Bug two: `safe_substitute` hides missing fields.** Where `substitute` raises on a missing field, `safe_substitute` leaves the literal `$topic` in the text. That goes to the model as a prompt containing `$topic`, and you get a confident answer about nothing, with no error anywhere.

```python
from string import Template


def render(text: str, values: dict) -> str:
    """Fill a template, warning about values the template does not use."""
    template = Template(text)

    used = {name for name in values if "$" + name in text}
    unused = set(values) - used
    if unused:
        print(f"warning: unused values: {sorted(unused)}")

    return template.substitute(values)
```

The second bug is the dangerous one, and `safe_substitute` is a trap precisely because of its name. "Safe" means it will not raise. For a prompt, not raising is the unsafe behaviour -- a loud failure is far better than silently sending a broken prompt and getting plausible output back.
:::

## What to remember

- A template is a good prompt with the changing parts marked
- All the instructions live in the fixed part, never in what the caller remembers to add
- Build against three or four different inputs, including an awkward one
- Use `string.Template` when the prompt contains literal braces
- Prefer a loud failure over silently sending a broken prompt

lessons.title: Iterative prompting
lessons.description: Diagnose, change one thing, re-run -- and do not tune to a single input.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Almost nobody writes a good prompt first time. The skill is not writing the perfect prompt; it is improving one efficiently.

### The loop

1. Write a reasonable first attempt
2. Run it on a **real** input
3. Identify what is specifically wrong
4. Change **one thing**
5. Run again on the same input
6. Repeat until good enough, then test on different inputs

Steps 3 and 4 are where people go wrong.

### Diagnose before you change

"That is not what I wanted" is not a diagnosis. Before editing, name the problem precisely:

- **Too long or short?** A length constraint is missing.
- **Wrong tone?** The audience is unspecified, or a role would help.
- **Missing something?** State the requirement explicitly.
- **Made something up?** Supply the source, add the uncertainty instruction.
- **Wrong shape?** The format is unspecified.
- **Misunderstood the task?** Your instruction is ambiguous. Reread it as a stranger would.
- **Right but generic?** Not enough context about your specific situation.

Each diagnosis points at a different fix. Guessing wastes rounds.

### Change one thing at a time

When you change four things and the output improves, you have learned nothing. You do not know which change helped, which did nothing, and which made it worse while another change compensated.

This feels slow and is faster, because you end with a prompt where every line is earning its place.

### Two ways to iterate

**Editing the prompt** is the main one, and what you keep.

**Correcting in conversation** -- "make that shorter", "add a section on cost" -- is useful for exploring what you want. But remember module 2: none of it persists. When you find the version you like, **fold the corrections back into the prompt**.

A very effective trick: converse until the output is right, then ask the model to write the prompt that would have produced it in one shot. Then test that prompt on a fresh input. It is often a good starting draft.

### Knowing when to stop

Stop when the output is good enough for its purpose, not when it is perfect.

A prompt that needs a small edit each time may be entirely fine. Polishing a prompt for an hour to save thirty seconds of editing, on something you will run twice, is a poor trade. Judge by how often you will run it.

### Watch for overfitting

If you tune a prompt against one input, you will end up with a prompt that works on that input.

Once it is good, test on three or four different inputs, including an awkward one. Prompts that were beautifully tuned on a single example routinely fall apart on the second.

## Demonstrate

A real iteration, over four rounds.

**Round 1.** *"Summarise this article."*
Output: eight paragraphs, longer than useful. **Diagnosis:** no length constraint.

**Round 2.** *"Summarise this article in under 150 words."*
Output: right length, but leads with background and buries the finding. **Diagnosis:** no priority stated.

**Round 3.** *"Summarise this article in under 150 words. Lead with the main finding."*
Output: good, but includes a statistic the article attributed to someone else, stated as the article's own. **Diagnosis:** no attribution instruction.

**Round 4.** *"Summarise this article in under 150 words. Lead with the main finding. Where the article cites another source for a claim, say so. Use only what is in the article."*
Output: usable.

Four rounds, one change each, each fixing a named problem. The final prompt has four clauses and every one of them is there for a reason you could explain.

Compare that with adding six clauses at once and never knowing which mattered.

## Practice

Take a prompt of yours that gives mediocre output.

Run it and write down, in one sentence, exactly what is wrong. Not "it is bad" -- which of the seven diagnoses above applies.

Make one change. Run again. Record.

Repeat at least four times, keeping every version and every output.

Then take your final prompt and run it on two inputs you have never used. If it falls apart, you overfitted, and the fix is to iterate again across all three inputs at once.

## What to remember

- Diagnose the specific problem before changing anything
- Change one thing per round so you learn what each change did
- Conversational corrections do not persist; fold them back into the prompt
- Ask the model to write the prompt that would have produced a good output
- Test on several inputs at the end or you will have tuned to one

lessons.title: Common prompting mistakes
lessons.description: Ten failures that account for most disappointing output.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Ten mistakes account for most disappointing output. Most people make several at once.

### 1. Assuming context the model does not have

You know the project, the people, the constraints. The model knows only what you typed. "Can you look at the deck and tell me if it works" means nothing without the deck and without knowing what "works" would mean.

### 2. Asking several things at once

"Summarise this, translate it, and suggest improvements" gets you a mediocre version of all three. Separate requests, or explicit numbered sections.

### 3. Leaving the format unspecified

If you do not say, you get whatever the model defaults to, and it changes between runs. Any time you will do something with the output, specify the shape.

### 4. Prohibitions where specifications would work

"Do not be too formal" tells the model where not to go. "Write as you would to a colleague you know well" tells it where to go. Positive instructions land more reliably.

### 5. Relying on recall instead of supplying the source

Asking about a document instead of pasting it. Asking for facts instead of providing them. This is the single largest source of hallucination in everyday use, and it is entirely avoidable.

### 6. Believing the confidence

No amount of assured tone means anything. This is worth restating as a prompting mistake because it changes behaviour: people stop checking when the output sounds certain, which is exactly backwards.

### 7. Not saying what to do when the answer is unknown

Without an explicit instruction, uncertainty gets resolved as invention. One sentence prevents it.

### 8. Tuning on one example

Covered in the last lesson, and worth repeating because it is so common. A prompt perfected on a single input is a prompt that works on a single input.

### 9. Cargo-culting magic phrases

"Take a deep breath." "This is very important to my career." "You are the world's greatest expert." These circulate widely. Some had measurable effects on specific older models. Most do nothing now, and none of them substitute for saying clearly what you want.

If you use one, test whether it actually helps on your task. Usually it does not.

### 10. Long conversations where a fresh one would be better

Conversations accumulate. Earlier context shapes later output in ways you stop tracking, and eventually the window overflows and things silently drop.

When you switch topic, or the output starts drifting oddly, start a new conversation with a clean prompt. It is nearly always faster than trying to steer a long one back.

### The shortest useful checklist

Before sending anything important:

- Have I supplied the material, or am I relying on recall?
- Have I said who this is for?
- Have I said how long, and in what shape?
- Have I said what to do if it does not know?
- Am I asking one thing or several?

## Demonstrate

One prompt with six of these mistakes, and the repair.

**Before.**

> Can you review the proposal and make it better? Don't make it too long or too corporate, and don't use jargon. Also translate the summary into Hindi. You are an expert business consultant.

Mistakes: no proposal supplied (1), three tasks at once (2), no format (3), three prohibitions and no specifications (4), empty expertise claim (9), no instruction for the unknown (7).

**After.** Two separate requests.

> Below is a project proposal for an internal audience of department heads.
>
> [proposal text]
>
> Review it for clarity and persuasiveness. For each issue, quote the sentence, say what is unclear, and suggest a replacement. Write as you would to a colleague you know well: direct, specific, no hedging.
>
> Where the proposal makes a claim it does not support, flag it rather than rewriting it -- I need to know what is missing, not have it smoothed over.
>
> Format: a numbered list, at most eight items, most important first.

Then, separately, the translation.

The second version is longer. It also works on the first attempt, which the first version never would.

## Practice

Take five prompts you have actually used. Old chat history is ideal.

Mark each against the ten mistakes. Count how many you find.

Most people find between two and four per prompt, and find that mistakes 1, 3 and 7 dominate.

Now rewrite the worst one using the checklist, and run both versions on the same input.

## What to remember

- Missing context and missing format cause most disappointing output
- Ask one thing at a time
- Prefer specifications over prohibitions
- Always say what to do when the answer is not available
- Magic phrases are folklore; test them or drop them
- Start a fresh conversation more often than feels necessary

lessons.title: Evaluating a prompt
lessons.description: Turning 'it seems better' into a number you can defend.
lessons.content:
## Learn

You cannot improve what you do not measure. Prompt evaluation means deciding, in advance and in writing, what a good output looks like -- then checking against it.

Without this, "the new prompt seems better" is a feeling, and feelings are heavily influenced by which version you wrote most recently.

### The minimum viable evaluation

You do not need a framework. You need:

**1. A set of real inputs.** Ten is enough to start. Real ones, covering the variety you will actually see, including at least one awkward case.

**2. Criteria, written down before you look at any output.** Specific enough that two people would mark the same way.

**3. A score for each output against each criterion.** Pass or fail is fine. Three points is plenty.

**4. A record.** Prompt version, date, score. Otherwise you will not know whether you are improving.

That is it. An afternoon of setup, and it converts every future prompt decision from argument into evidence.

### Writing criteria that work

Bad criteria are the usual failure. "Is it good?" cannot be marked.

Turn each into something checkable:

- **Bad:** Is the summary accurate? **Good:** Does every factual claim appear in the source document?
- **Bad:** Is it the right length? **Good:** Is it under 150 words?
- **Bad:** Is the tone right? **Good:** Would you send this to a customer without editing?
- **Bad:** Is it useful? **Good:** Does it state a specific next action with an owner?

The test: could someone else apply this criterion and reach the same verdict? If not, sharpen it.

### What to measure

**Correctness.** Is it right? Verify, do not assume.

**Completeness.** Did it get everything required?

**Format.** Does it match the shape you asked for? Easy to check automatically, and prompts drift here more than people expect.

**Invention.** Did it add anything not in the source? Mark this separately -- it is the most dangerous failure and the easiest to miss, because invented content often reads well.

**Consistency.** Run the same input three times. Do you get comparable output? High variation is a real problem for anything you intend to rely on.

### The trap

**Do not write your criteria after seeing the output.** You will unconsciously write criteria the output happens to meet.

Write them first, against the task. If the output reveals a criterion you had not thought of, add it -- and then re-mark every version against the new list, including ones you already scored.

### Automating the easy parts

Some criteria are checkable by code: length, required sections present, valid JSON, no forbidden phrase. Automate those and spend your attention on the ones needing judgement.

## Demonstrate

Evaluating a meeting-summary prompt.

**Inputs:** ten real transcripts. Two are messy -- one has no clear decisions, one has an unnamed speaker.

**Criteria, written before running anything:**

1. Under 250 words
2. Every action item in the transcript appears in the summary
3. Every action item has an owner, or says "owner not stated"
4. No claim appears that is not supported by the transcript
5. Output has the three required sections
6. Where there were no decisions, it says so rather than inventing one

Criteria 1 and 5 are automatable. Criteria 2, 3, 4 and 6 need a person, and criterion 4 needs a careful one.

**Result of version 1:** 10/10 on length, 7/10 on completeness, 4/10 on owners, 9/10 on invention, 10/10 on sections, 0/2 on the no-decisions case.

That last number is the finding. On both transcripts with no real decisions, the prompt invented one. You would never have discovered that by running it on a normal transcript and thinking the output looked good.

## Practice

### Exercise: an automatic checker

Write a function that runs the automatable checks against a summary and returns which passed.

```python
def check_summary(text: str, max_words: int = 250) -> dict[str, bool]:
    """Run the automatable checks against a generated summary.

    Checks: within the word limit, has all three required sections,
    and does not contain hedging phrases we have banned.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for a good summary:

```
{'within_word_limit': True, 'has_all_sections': True, 'no_banned_phrases': True}
```

:::hint Getting started
Three independent checks, each producing a bool. Word count is `len(text.split())`. For sections, define the required headings as a constant and check each appears -- compare case-insensitively, since a model may capitalise differently. For banned phrases, check that none appears in the lowercased text.
:::

:::solution
```python
REQUIRED_SECTIONS = ("summary", "decisions", "action items")
BANNED_PHRASES = ("it seems", "it appears that", "one could argue", "as an ai")


def check_summary(text: str, max_words: int = 250) -> dict[str, bool]:
    """Run the automatable checks against a generated summary."""
    lowered = text.lower()

    return {
        "within_word_limit": len(text.split()) <= max_words,
        "has_all_sections": all(section in lowered for section in REQUIRED_SECTIONS),
        "no_banned_phrases": not any(phrase in lowered for phrase in BANNED_PHRASES),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    good = "Summary\nWe agreed the date.\n\nDecisions\n- Ship on Friday\n\nAction items\n- Ana to email"
    print(check_summary(good))
    print(check_summary("It seems the team met. " * 200))
```

Output:

```
{'within_word_limit': True, 'has_all_sections': True, 'no_banned_phrases': True}
{'within_word_limit': False, 'has_all_sections': False, 'no_banned_phrases': False}
```

Lowercasing once at the top rather than inside each comprehension is worth doing -- it is clearer, and it avoids repeating the work on a long summary. Returning a dict rather than a single bool means a failing run tells you which check failed, which is the whole point of running checks.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This function is meant to report the pass rate per criterion across many runs. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def pass_rates(results: list[dict[str, bool]]) -> dict[str, float]:
    rates = {}
    for result in results:
        for name, passed in result.items():
            if passed:
                rates[name] = rates.get(name, 0) + 1
    return {name: count / len(results) for name, count in rates.items()}
```

:::hint What to look at
Run it on a criterion that failed every single time. Then run it on an empty list of results.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: a criterion that never passes disappears from the report.** `rates` is only written to inside `if passed`, so a check failing on every run has no key at all and is silently absent from the output -- the single most important thing to see is the one thing the report omits.

**Bug two: an empty results list raises `ZeroDivisionError`.** The final comprehension divides by `len(results)` with no guard.

```python
def pass_rates(results: list[dict[str, bool]]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Pass rate per criterion, including criteria that never passed."""
    if not results:
        return {}

    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for result in results:
        for name, passed in result.items():
            counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + int(passed)

    return {name: count / len(results) for name, count in counts.items()}
```

Moving the increment outside the `if` and adding `int(passed)` registers every criterion on first sight, whether it passed or not. Bug one is the instructive one: the code runs, produces a clean-looking report, and quietly hides your worst result. A report that omits its own failures is worse than no report, because you trust it.
:::

## What to remember

- Ten real inputs, written criteria, and a record beats any amount of impression
- Criteria must be specific enough that two people would mark the same way
- Write criteria before seeing output, and re-mark everything when you add one
- Measure invention separately; it is the most dangerous and best-hidden failure
- Automate the checkable criteria and spend judgement on the rest

lessons.title: Five real prompts, start to finish
lessons.description: Marketing, research, CV, SQL and data analysis, weak version and strong.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Five prompts from the source outline, each worked properly. These are the shapes you will reuse most.

For each: the weak version, the strong version, and what specifically made the difference.

### 1. A marketing prompt

**Weak.** *"Write marketing copy for our app."*

**Strong.**

> Our product is a mobile app that helps college students track shared expenses with flatmates. It is free, and it works offline.
>
> Write three versions of a 30-word app store description, aimed at first-year undergraduates in India who have just moved into shared accommodation.
>
> Each version should lead with a different benefit: one on avoiding arguments, one on the free price, one on offline use.
>
> Plain language. No exclamation marks. Do not claim anything the description above does not support.
>
> Format: numbered 1 to 3, each on one line.

**The difference:** the product described, the audience named, three variants requested with the angle specified for each, a constraint against invented claims, and a format. Six pieces of information the weak version left to chance.

### 2. A research prompt

**Weak.** *"Tell me about the effects of remote work on productivity."*

**Strong.**

> I am writing a literature review on remote work and productivity for an undergraduate management course.
>
> Give me an overview of the main positions in this debate. For each position: what it claims, what kind of evidence supports it, and what its critics say.
>
> Do not cite specific papers, authors or statistics -- I will find those myself. If you name a study, I have no way to check it and would rather you did not.
>
> Where the evidence is genuinely mixed, say so rather than presenting a consensus that does not exist.
>
> Format: one section per position, at most four, each under 150 words.

**The difference:** and it is the important one -- this prompt **removes the hallucination risk by not asking for the thing that hallucinates**. Citations and statistics are where invention clusters. Asking for the shape of a debate and finding the sources yourself gets the value without the risk.

### 3. A CV prompt

**Weak.** *"Write me a CV."*

**Strong.**

> Below is my current CV and a job description I am applying for.
>
> CV:
> [text]
>
> Job description:
> [text]
>
> Rewrite the summary paragraph and the bullet points under each role so they speak to this job description.
>
> Rules:
> - Use only facts already in my CV. Do not add skills, tools, achievements or dates.
> - Where the job asks for something my CV does not evidence, list it separately at the end under "gaps" rather than inventing coverage.
> - Each bullet under 20 words, starting with a verb.
> - Keep my dates and job titles exactly as written.

**The difference:** the "use only facts already present" rule is doing all the work. Without it, models routinely produce a CV with invented achievements, which is both useless and a genuinely serious thing to send to an employer. The "gaps" section converts a temptation to invent into useful information.

### 4. A SQL and Python prompt

**Weak.** *"Write a query to get top customers."*

**Strong.**

> I have a PostgreSQL database with these tables:
>
> ```
> customers (id, name, country, created_at)
> orders (id, customer_id, total_amount, status, created_at)
> ```
>
> Write a query returning the 10 customers with the highest total value of completed orders in the last 12 months, with their name, country and that total.
>
> Notes:
> - status is 'completed', 'pending' or 'cancelled'
> - include customers with no qualifying orders only if they would otherwise rank in the top 10, otherwise exclude them
> - explain the query in two sentences after the SQL
>
> If anything in this specification is ambiguous, say so instead of choosing for me.

**The difference:** the schema is supplied, the valid values are stated, the edge case is decided explicitly, and ambiguity is surfaced rather than silently resolved. Most bad generated SQL comes from a model guessing a schema and a convention.

### 5. A data analysis prompt

**Weak.** *"Analyse this data."*

**Strong.**

> Below is a CSV of monthly sales by region for the last two years.
>
> [data]
>
> I need to brief a sales director who has ten minutes and no statistics background.
>
> Tell me:
> 1. The three most notable patterns, each with the numbers that show it
> 2. Anything that looks like an error in the data rather than a real pattern
> 3. The single question I should ask the regional teams
>
> Rules:
> - Quote actual figures from the data for every claim
> - Do not calculate growth rates or averages yourself beyond simple sums -- flag what should be calculated properly and I will do it
> - If the data is too sparse to support a claim, say so

**The difference:** the audience is named, three specific outputs are requested, and -- most importantly -- the prompt **restricts the model to the arithmetic it is reliable at**. Asking a language model for careful calculation is asking for the thing it is worst at. Asking it to spot patterns and flag what needs proper calculation plays to what it is good at.

### The pattern across all five

Every strong version does the same four things:

1. **Supplies the material** rather than relying on recall
2. **Names the audience and purpose**
3. **States what to do when uncertain** instead of letting it invent
4. **Avoids asking for the thing the model is worst at** -- citations, precise arithmetic, facts it would have to remember

That fourth point is the most advanced idea in this module. Good prompting is partly about writing clearly, and partly about **not asking for what the tool cannot do**.

## Demonstrate

Take the research prompt. Run both versions.

The weak one will very likely produce named studies with authors and years. Look three of them up.

The strong one produces the structure of the debate and no citations at all. It is less impressive-looking and far more useful, because everything in it is something you can act on.

That comparison is the whole lesson.

## Practice

Pick the one of the five closest to something you actually do.

Write your own strong version for your real situation, using all four of the pattern points above.

Run it against a weak version of the same request. Then, critically, **verify the weak version's output** -- look up its citations, check its arithmetic, confirm its claims.

Record how long the verification took. That is the hidden cost of a weak prompt, and it is usually much larger than the time saved writing it.

## What to remember

- Supply the material, name the audience, handle uncertainty, restrict the format
- Do not ask for citations you cannot check; ask for the shape and find sources yourself
- On a CV, "use only facts already present" prevents a serious failure
- Supply the schema and the conventions before asking for code
- Do not ask a language model for careful arithmetic; ask it to flag what needs calculating

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 4.

:::quiz
Q. What does "the prompt" actually consist of?
- The question you type
+ Everything sent to the model: standing instructions, conversation so far, pasted material and your question
- The system prompt only
- Your question plus the model's previous answer
= Thinking of the prompt as just your question limits you to rewording, which is the weakest lever. Understanding it as everything sent opens up the large levers: supplying material, giving examples, setting constraints and format.

Q. Which part of a prompt is most commonly missing when output disappoints?
- Role
- Format
+ Context
- Examples
= Missing context is the most common cause. People know their own situation so well that they forget the model knows only what was typed. Supplying the material is usually the single biggest improvement available.

Q. Where should long context go relative to the instruction?
+ Before the instruction
- After the instruction
- Split either side of it
- It makes no difference
= With a long document, putting the instruction after the material works noticeably better -- the model reads the material and then learns what to do with it. Burying the instruction thousands of words back performs worse.

Q. Why do few-shot examples often succeed where instructions fail?
- The model learns from the examples and updates its weights
+ They make the pattern you want the most likely continuation
- Examples use fewer tokens than instructions
- The model trusts examples more than instructions
= Nothing is learned; the weights never change. Examples work because a model predicts continuations, and after three cases of a pattern the fourth is the overwhelmingly obvious thing to produce. It is also far easier to demonstrate a tone than describe one.

Q. What does role prompting actually change?
- The model's knowledge in that domain
- The reliability of the answer
+ The tone, vocabulary and perspective of the output
- The model's willingness to admit uncertainty
= A role shifts which region of language the output is drawn from. It adds no knowledge and no reliability. Claiming expertise can make a wrong answer sound more authoritative, which is worse than useless.

Q. Why does writing out reasoning steps improve hard answers?
- It gives the model more time to process
+ Each step becomes part of the context conditioning the next, so the answer is produced in the presence of the working
- It triggers a more capable mode in the model
- It reduces the number of tokens needed
= The model produces text token by token, each conditioned on what came before. Jumping straight to an answer means no intermediate work exists to condition on. The working is not hidden, it is the output.

Q. Which single line does most to prevent invented values in a structured extraction?
- "Return only valid JSON"
- "Be accurate"
+ "If a field is not stated, use null. Do not infer."
- "You are a careful data analyst"
= Without it, a missing field gets a plausible invented value. That is far harder to catch than ordinary hallucination, because the JSON parses perfectly and the value looks extracted rather than generated.

Q. Why use `string.Template` rather than `str.format` for prompt templates?
- It is faster
+ Prompts often contain literal braces, such as JSON examples, which `str.format` would try to interpret as fields
- It supports more data types
- `str.format` cannot handle multi-line strings
= This bites the first time you put a JSON shape into a prompt template. `string.Template` uses `$name` and leaves braces alone.

Q. You changed four things in a prompt and the output improved. What have you learned?
- All four changes helped
+ Very little -- you cannot tell which change helped, which did nothing, and which hurt
- The prompt is now optimal
- The first change was the important one
= Changing one thing per round feels slower and is faster, because you end with a prompt where every clause is earning its place and you know why it is there.

Q. When should you write your evaluation criteria?
- After seeing the first output, so they are realistic
+ Before running anything, against the task
- After comparing two prompt versions
- Criteria are not needed if you have enough examples
= Criteria written after seeing output are unconsciously shaped to what the output happened to do. Write them first. If output reveals a criterion you missed, add it and re-mark every version, including ones already scored.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 5. Below that, revisit the lesson covering what you missed. Everything from module 6 onward assumes you can write a prompt with context, constraints, format and an uncertainty instruction without being reminded.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: building a reusable prompt template
lessons.description: Build, test and iterate a template for something you actually do.
lessons.content:
Forty-five minutes. You will finish with a tested, reusable template for something you actually do, plus the evidence that it works.

## Before you start

Choose a task you do **repeatedly**. That word matters -- a template for something you do once is wasted effort.

Good candidates: summarising meetings, replying to a recurring type of enquiry, turning notes into a structured format, reviewing a document against a checklist, drafting a recurring report section.

You need **four real inputs** for the task. Real ones, anonymised if necessary. At least one should be awkward: incomplete, messy, or a case where the right answer is "there is nothing here".

## Step 1: Criteria first

Before writing any prompt, write five to seven criteria a good output must meet.

Make them checkable. "Is it good" is not a criterion; "under 200 words", "every action has an owner or says owner not stated", "no claim appears that is not in the source" are.

Mark each as automatable or needing judgement.

## Step 2: First draft

Write your template using the six parts from lesson 2: role if useful, context, task, constraints, format, examples if needed.

Mark the variable parts with `$name`.

Include the uncertainty instruction. Include what to do with the awkward case you identified.

## Step 3: Run on all four

Fill the template for each of your four inputs and run them.

Score every output against every criterion. Record the numbers. You will have a grid of four runs by six or so criteria.

## Step 4: Iterate, one change at a time

Find your worst criterion. Diagnose it using the list from lesson 8. Change **one** thing.

Re-run all four inputs. Re-score.

Repeat at least three times. Keep every version of the template and every score grid.

:::hint Everything passes on the first try
Then your criteria are too easy or your inputs are too clean. Add a harder criterion -- most people can add "no claim appears that is not in the source" and immediately find failures. Or add a genuinely nasty input: an empty one, one in two languages, one where the right answer is that there is nothing to report.
:::

## Step 5: Build it as code

Turn your final template into a working function, using the `PromptTemplate` class from lesson 7 or your own.

It must:

- Raise clearly if a required field is missing or empty
- Apply sensible defaults for optional fields
- Be importable and callable from elsewhere

```python
from string import Template


class PromptTemplate:
    ...  # your implementation from lesson 7


MY_TEMPLATE = PromptTemplate(
    text="""...your prompt...""",
    required=[...],
    defaults={...},
)
```

## Step 6: Add the automatic checks

Write a `check()` function running your automatable criteria against an output, returning a dict of criterion name to pass or fail.

Run it against all four of your final outputs.

:::solution What a finished check function looks like
```python
REQUIRED_SECTIONS = ("summary", "actions")
BANNED = ("as an ai", "i cannot")


def check(text: str, max_words: int = 200) -> dict[str, bool]:
    """Automatable criteria for this template's output."""
    lowered = text.lower()
    return {
        "within_word_limit": len(text.split()) <= max_words,
        "has_sections": all(s in lowered for s in REQUIRED_SECTIONS),
        "no_banned_phrases": not any(b in lowered for b in BANNED),
        "not_empty": bool(text.strip()),
    }
```

Yours will differ -- these are your criteria, not mine. The shape is what matters: one dict, one key per criterion, a bool each, so a failure tells you which criterion failed rather than just that something did.
:::

## Step 7: Write it up

1. The task, and why a template is worth it
2. Your criteria, and which are automatable
3. Your score grid for version 1 and for your final version
4. Each change you made and which criterion it was fixing
5. The awkward input, and how your final template handles it
6. One thing still not good enough, and what you would try next

## What good looks like

A strong submission shows **the scores improving across versions**, with each improvement traceable to a named change. That is the evidence that you iterated rather than fiddled.

It also handles the awkward input properly. A template that only works on clean inputs is not finished, and the awkward case is where almost all the learning is.

lessons.title: Assignment: a prompt library with evaluations
lessons.description: Three tested prompts plus working code, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Build a **prompt library**: three tested, documented, reusable prompts for tasks you genuinely do, with the evidence that each one works.

This is the most directly useful thing you will produce in the first half of this course. People who do it properly keep using it.

## What to submit

One document plus one Python file.

### The document, 1000 to 1400 words

**1. The three tasks.** What each prompt is for, who would use it, and how often. One paragraph each.

They must be genuinely different in shape. Three variations on "summarise this" is one prompt, not three. Aim for a mix -- something that produces prose, something that produces structured output, something that makes a judgement or applies a checklist.

**2. The prompts themselves.** Each in full, with the variable parts marked.

For each, a short note on why it is built that way: which of the six parts you included, which you left out and why.

**3. The evaluation.** For each prompt:

- Your criteria, written before you tested
- How many real inputs you tested on -- **minimum four per prompt**
- A score grid: inputs against criteria
- At least one full example: the filled prompt, the output, your marking

**4. The iteration.** For at least one prompt, show the version history. What version 1 looked like, what was wrong, what you changed, what happened. Three versions minimum.

**5. Honest limits.** For each prompt, one situation where it does not work well, and what you would do instead. Every prompt has one. Finding it is the sign you tested properly.

### The Python file

A working module containing:

- Your three templates, using a `PromptTemplate` class or equivalent
- A `check()` function per prompt running the automatable criteria
- A `__main__` block demonstrating each one on a sample input

It must run. A file that raises on import scores nothing for this part.

```python
"""My prompt library."""

from string import Template


class PromptTemplate:
    ...


MEETING_SUMMARY = PromptTemplate(...)
EMAIL_TRIAGE = PromptTemplate(...)
DOC_REVIEW = PromptTemplate(...)


def check_meeting_summary(text: str) -> dict[str, bool]:
    ...


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(MEETING_SUMMARY.render(...))
```

**No API keys in the file.** If you call an API, read the key from the environment with `os.environ`. A key written into a submitted file loses marks and, more importantly, is a real security incident once that file goes anywhere.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Task selection, 10 marks.** Full marks for three genuinely different, genuinely recurring tasks. Marks lost for three variations of the same thing, or tasks nobody would actually repeat.

**Prompt quality, 20 marks.** Full marks where each prompt supplies context, names its audience, states constraints and format, and handles the uncertain case. Marks lost for any prompt missing the uncertainty instruction, and for prohibitions where specifications would work.

**Evaluation, 30 marks.** Full marks for criteria written in advance, at least four real inputs per prompt, a complete score grid, and one fully worked example per prompt. This is the heaviest section because it is the difference between three prompts and a prompt library. Criteria that could not be marked consistently by two people lose marks here.

**Iteration evidence, 15 marks.** Full marks for three versions of at least one prompt, each change tied to a named problem and followed by a re-score. Marks lost where several things changed at once, since that shows nothing was learned.

**The code, 15 marks.** Full marks for a module that runs, raises clearly on missing required fields, and includes working checks. Marks lost for a file that does not run, for `safe_substitute` hiding a missing field, and heavily for any hard-coded key.

**Honest limits, 10 marks.** Full marks for a real, specific failure case per prompt with a stated alternative. Marks lost for "it sometimes needs editing", which is true of everything and says nothing.

## What will cost you marks

**Criteria written after seeing the output.** Usually obvious: the criteria match what the output happened to do, and everything passes on version 1. If everything passed immediately, say so and explain why you believe the criteria were hard enough.

**Testing on one input per prompt.** The minimum is four, and at least one awkward.

**Claiming an improvement with no before-and-after score.** "This version is much better" is not evidence.

**A hard-coded API key.** This costs marks in two sections and is worth checking twice before you submit.

:::hint I cannot think of three different enough tasks
Look at what you do weekly rather than what sounds impressive. Some that work well: turning lecture notes into revision questions; drafting the reply to a recurring type of email; checking a document against a submission checklist; extracting structured fields from messy text someone sends you; summarising a long thread for someone who was not on it; converting rough bullet points into a paragraph in your own voice. Pick three with different output shapes -- prose, structured data, and a judgement.
:::
